Davidson County by the numbers

Which Metro offices deal with a Davidson County tax bill?

Two Metro Nashville offices split the job. The Assessor of Property appraises and classifies every parcel, while the Office of the Metropolitan Trustee sends the statements and takes the payments. The Trustee has no authority over the amount of an assessment.

Each September the Trustee receives the certified roll from the Assessor. The Trustee's office is in the Howard Office Building at 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 220, open weekdays from 8 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon. The Assessor's office takes value questions at 615-862-6080.

Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville are the only cities in Davidson County that bill separate city taxes. Their numbers are 615-297-6041, 615-859-0596 and 615-851-2200. Taxes for every other city address are collected by the Metropolitan Trustee.

What is the Davidson County payment calendar?

Statements go into the mail during the first week of October. Payment opens the first Monday of that month, and the full amount has to be in by the final day of February if you want to skip interest.

Because today is November 15, 2026, the 2026 bill is already out and the cutoff arrives in late February 2027. You may pay in installments along the way.

Miss the cutoff and interest of 1.5% (18% a year) is added to the base tax on the first of every month, beginning March 1. The Trustee's collections division works delinquent accounts from March through the following February, and after that the Clerk and Master's office collects them.

How do payments reach the Metropolitan Trustee?

Options include the Trustee's website, the mail, and the counter at the Howard Office Building. Payments sent through your own bank's bill pay count on the day the Trustee receives them.

  • Make checks payable to Metropolitan Trustee, PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.
  • Cards cost 2.35% of the payment, with a $2.00 floor, and an E-Check costs $1.00. Metro keeps none of it.
  • A postmark sets the payment date for mail, but a private meter stamp does not. With no postmark, the day the envelope arrives counts.
  • A website payment is credited on the day you make it.

The Trustee's pages call out that new owners should check their closing statement or ask the title company who owes the tax, because unpaid taxes continue to accrue against the property.

What changed in the 2025 reappraisal?

The Assessor's final countywide median value increase was 45% as of January 1, 2025. Notices were mailed April 18, 2025, four years after the previous reappraisal in 2021, and the Assessor said owners were being given more time than usual to appeal.

State law requires a Certified Tax Rate after each reappraisal so that local governments do not collect a windfall on existing property. The 2025 rates came to $2.782 per $100 in the General Services District and $2.814 per $100 in the Urban Services District, down from $2.922 and $3.254 in 2024.

Davidson County tax rates per $100 of assessed value

2025$2.782$2.814
2024$2.922$3.254
2021$2.953$3.288
2020$3.788$4.221

Source: Davidson County Assessor, Tax Rates and Calculator. The Urban Services District pays for garbage pickup, street lights and sidewalks that owners in the General Services District arrange on their own.

How do you work out a Davidson County bill?

Multiply the appraised value by the 25% residential ratio and apply the rate for your district. The Assessor's own example uses a $400,000 house in the Urban Services District: $400,000 times 25% is $100,000 of assessed value, and at $2.814 per $100 the bill is $2,814.00.

Your notice shows a Tax Jurisdiction box that says whether you are in the GSD, the USD or one of the satellite cities. Those are Ridgetop, Goodlettsville, Belle Meade, Berry Hill, Forest Hills and Oak Hill, and their owners pay the GSD rate plus the city's own rate. Downtown properties may also sit inside the Central Business Improvement District or the Gulch Business Improvement District, which add their own assessments.

What is the path to contest a Davidson County value?

The Assessor handles an informal review first. A formal appeal then goes before an independent hearing officer or the Metropolitan Board of Equalization, scheduled through the Assessor's call center at 615-862-6059.

For the 2025 cycle, informal reviews had to be requested by May 9 and formal appeals scheduled by 4:00 p.m. on June 27. The Assessor warned that owners who miss the formal deadline may lose their right to appeal for that tax year. Those dates are past, so a challenge today applies to a future year.

During an appeal the Trustee says to pay at least the undisputed share before delinquency, along with any past-due prior-year tax. To find the undisputed portion, divide the value you claim by the Assessor's value and multiply by the tax due. A final certificate of assessment brings either a refund or a balance owed with interest at the Federal Reserve composite prime rate minus two points.

What tax relief can a Davidson County owner claim?

The state reimburses local taxes for low-income elderly or disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans, and the Trustee runs a tax freeze for owners 65 and older. Eligibility turns on age or disability, ownership and residency, and income.

  • Elderly and disabled relief: applicants must turn 65 by December 31 of the tax year or be disabled by that date, and must document ownership with a bill, deed or probated will.
  • Disabled veterans: a 100% disability rating is required, there is no income limit, and relief covers the first $175,000 of market value.
  • Tax freeze: owners 65 and older who live in the home can freeze the bill at the amount for the year they qualify. Applications are due by April 5 each year, and the Trustee's number is 615-862-6330.

Income caps on the Trustee's page are stated for the 2020 calendar year, so ask the Trustee for the current limits before you apply.

What does Nashville-Davidson look like for a seller?

Davidson County is governed as Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson County. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 745,904 residents, up 4.2% from April 2020, spread over 503.70 square miles of land at roughly 1,421 per square mile.

Census QuickFacts shows the following figures for 2020 to 2024:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $417,400.
  • Share of housing lived in by owners: 52.8%, which leaves renters near half of households.
  • Median gross rent: $1,582.
  • Median household income: $77,853.
  • Households: 324,907, in 389,379 housing units as of July 2025.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 5,632.

Source: Census QuickFacts. The Register of Deeds, Karen Johnson, is at 300 Deaderick Street in Nashville and records deeds for sales anywhere in the county.

What happens to a delinquent Davidson County parcel?

Delinquent parcels can end up in a tax sale auction run through Chancery Court. Auctions are held one Wednesday a month starting in June, and sales are final, but the owner has a one-year right to redeem the property. The buyer earns 10% annual interest on the purchase price during the redemption period.

The Trustee's page says the county does not help purchasers with any foreclosure or eviction. Anyone running behind should phone the Trustee's collections division before March 1 for a payoff figure, and a seller should hand that number to the title company.

More questions about Davidson County, TN Property Tax Guide

When is Davidson County property tax due?

Statements go out the first week of October, taxes are payable from the first Monday of October, and the full amount must be paid by the last day of February to avoid interest. Interest of 1.5% per month starts March 1.

What is the Davidson County property tax rate?

For 2025 the General Services District rate is $2.782 per $100 of assessed value and the Urban Services District rate is $2.814, according to the Assessor. Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville bill separate city taxes on top of the GSD rate.

How much did Davidson County values rise in the 2025 reappraisal?

The Assessor's final countywide median increase was 45% as of January 1, 2025. Council district medians ranged from 38% to 54%. The Certified Tax Rate was then set to keep revenue on existing property level.

Does Davidson County accept partial property tax payments?

Yes. The Trustee accepts partial payments during the collection period, but the full balance must be paid by the last day of February to avoid interest. Cards carry a 2.35% fee with a $2.00 minimum, and E-Check costs $1.00.

Who pays the property tax when a Davidson County house is sold?

The closing statement answers that. The Trustee tells new owners to check it or ask the title company, because payment depends on when the property is transferred and unpaid taxes continue to accrue against the property.

Knox County by the numbers

Which Knox County offices deal with property tax?

Two offices share the job, both in the Knoxville City-County Building at 400 Main Street. The Property Assessor, reachable at 865-215-2360, sets values and fields appeal questions. The Trustee, in Suite 427 at 865-215-2305, takes the payments. Each keeps weekday counter hours that start at eight and end at half past four. The Assessor's separate line for business personal property is 865-215-2362.

The Trustee's payment page lists six locations, plus these ways to pay:

  • Online through the county's property tax lookup, with a 2.5% processing fee on cards and $1.00 on e-checks
  • By phone at 865-215-2305, option 3
  • By mail to P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901

The Trustee describes its office as one that collects and accounts for over $1 billion a year in state, federal and local funds, so the same counter that takes a homeowner's check also handles county government's money. The Trustee's office also accepts address changes online, and the Assessor takes mailing address changes at 865-215-2360.

What is Knox County's tax rate this year?

The county finance page says taxes for fiscal 2026 are levied at $1.5540 per $100 of assessed value, set by the County Commission as part of the budget. Residential property is assessed at 25% of value, commercial at 40% and business personal property at 30%, and the Assessor's FAQ shows the formula: assessed value times the percentage times the combined city and county rate.

Take a house appraised at $300,000. A quarter of that is $75,000 of assessment, and at $1.5540 per $100 the county tax comes to $1,165.50. A home inside Knoxville adds the city's rate on top, because county residents who live in the city pay both. The county page does not print the city rate, so ask the City of Knoxville for it.

Source: Knox County Finance, General Information page.

What dates matter on the Knox County tax calendar?

The Assessor's calendar page maps out the tax year. Current-year taxes become due on October 1, and the final day for payment with no penalty or interest is February 28. March 1 is the delinquency date for the prior year. Today is November 15, 2026, so a 2026 bill is open and payable through the last day of February 2027.

The assessment side runs on its own clock:

  • January 1 is the assessment date for ownership and condition
  • March 15 is the greenbelt application deadline
  • May 20 is the deadline to apply for exemptions, and assessment change notices should be mailed by then
  • June 1 starts the County Board of Equalization, which meets through June
  • August 1 is the general deadline for State Board appeals, or 45 days after the county board's notice, whichever comes later

Knox County runs a two-year reappraisal cycle. Year one is field work and sales data, and year two applies the valuation models and mails new values with instructions for appeal. The county says reappraisal does not automatically raise taxes, because the Commission may adjust the rate afterward. The Assessor also hosts a property tax calculator and a parcel lookup, so an owner can check a value before the notice arrives.

Does Knox County offer tax relief or a freeze?

Yes, through the Trustee. The 2026 senior freeze is for owners who will be 65 or older by December 31, 2026, with combined 2025 income for the owner, spouse and all deed owners under $63,470, and VA income counts. State tax relief is available for disabled veterans, up to $444 for 2026 with no income limit, and for widows and widowers of a disabled veteran who have not remarried.

Relief is a state-funded payment credit and not an exemption, so the bill still arrives and must be paid. The enrollment window for the 2026 tax year runs from October 1, 2026 through April 5, 2027. The Trustee says the state sets that window, the county cannot change it, and no extensions are given. Applications cannot be accepted by email, but a form can be requested at taxrelief@knoxcounty.org or by calling 865-215-8554 for the recorded information line.

What is Knox County itself like?

Knox County was created on June 11, 1792, and covers 526 square miles, 508 of them land. It sits in the Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians, with long ridges such as Bays Mountain and Sharp's Ridge running northeast to southwest, and House Mountain at 2,064 feet is the high point. The Holston and French Broad rivers meet in the east of the county to form the Tennessee River, and that stretch is part of Fort Loudoun Lake. Knoxville is the county seat, and the town of Farragut is also within the county.

Census Bureau QuickFacts shows a growing market:

  • 511,453 residents on July 1, 2025, up 6.8% since April 2020
  • 65.2% owner-occupied, with a median home value of $320,900 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $74,222 and 12.8% of people in poverty
  • Median monthly owner cost of $1,589 with a mortgage and median rent of $1,261

The county's property assessor's office, tax offices and Metropolitan Planning Commission are combined between city and county, which is why a Knoxville homeowner deals with the same Trustee and Assessor as a rural owner.

What happens to Knox County property tax when a house is sold?

The Assessor sends a sales questionnaire whenever ownership changes, including private sales and transfers into a trust or estate. Once the Register of Deeds has the new deed on record, the Assessor changes the owner's name, which can take up to a week, and anyone still seeing the old name after a month should call 865-215-2360. Closing agents ask the Trustee for the payoff on the current year's bill and for any delinquent years.

Mid-year changes to a property are prorated under Tennessee Code section 67-5-603. A fire, demolition or finished addition between January 1 and September 1 changes the assessed value for part of that year only. A seller who rebuilt or tore down a structure should ask for a field review so the bill matches the house being sold.

The Trustee's tax sale page shows what happens to accounts that stay unpaid. The most recent sale listed was June 2, 2026, at The Grande Event Center on Clinton Highway, run through the Clerk and Master, and bidders had to be current on their own taxes. That date has passed, and the Trustee posts the next one when the court sets it.

More questions about Knox County, TN Property Tax Guide

When are Knox County property taxes due?

Current-year taxes become due and payable on October 1, and the final day for payment with no penalty or interest is February 28. March 1 is the delinquency date for the prior year's taxes.

What is the Knox County property tax rate?

The county levy for fiscal 2026 is $1.5540 per $100 of assessed value. A home inside a city also owes that city's rate, which the county page does not list.

Where does a Knox County owner file an assessment appeal?

Go first to the county board, which starts meeting June 1, and then to the state board by August 1 or 45 days after the county notice was sent. Before either, the Assessor at 865-215-2360 can arrange a field review.

What is the deadline for the Knox County senior tax freeze?

April 5, 2027 for the 2026 tax year. Applicants must be 65 or older by December 31, 2026, with 2025 combined income under $63,470.

Can I sell a Knox County house that owes property tax?

Yes. The Trustee supplies a payoff figure, and the closing agent clears it out of what the seller receives. Accounts left unpaid for years can end up at a court-run tax sale.

Shelby County by the numbers

Which Shelby County offices send and take property tax?

Shelby County divides the work among the Assessor of Property, the County Commission and the Trustee, and Memphis adds a second bill on top. The Assessor appraises every parcel, the Commission sets the county rate, and the Trustee applies that rate to each $100 of assessed value, then prints and mails the notices to the address the Assessor has on file. An escrow lender can pull the details and pay for the owner, in which case the notice is kept as a record.

  • Trustee: 157 Poplar Avenue, 2nd Floor, Memphis, TN 38103, phone (901) 222-0200, with counter service on weekdays from opening at eight until half past four. Payments by post go to P.O. Box 2751, Memphis, TN 38101-2751, and Regina Morrison Newman holds the Trustee's post.
  • Board of Equalization: 1075 Mullins Station Road, Suite C-142, Memphis, TN 38134, phone (901) 222-7300.
  • City of Memphis Treasury: 125 North Main Street, phone 901-522-1111, for the separate city bill.

The Trustee's realty tax page reminds owners to keep track of every parcel number they hold, and to look up the bill for any parcel whose notice does not arrive.

How big is Shelby County, and who lives there?

Shelby County is the westernmost county in Tennessee, bounded on the west by the Mississippi River, and it is both the most populous and the largest by area in the state. Its 781.6 square miles include Memphis, the county seat, along with the cities of Bartlett, Germantown, Lakeland and Millington and the towns of Arlington and Collierville. The lowest point in Tennessee is on the river in Shelby County, just outside the Memphis city limits. Since 2014 the suburbs have run their own school districts, while Shelby County Schools serves Memphis and most unincorporated areas.

QuickFacts from the Census Bureau show:

  • 910,226 people in July 2025, a 2.1% drop since the 2020 estimates base
  • 409,202 housing units, and an owner rate of 54.1%
  • $249,100 as the 2020 to 2024 median home value
  • $63,767 median household income and 19.0% of people below the poverty line
  • 1,230 building permits in 2025

Renters occupy about 46 percent of the county's homes, so a landlord selling a rental often has tax and tenant questions that an owner-occupant does not.

How are Shelby County property values set?

The Assessor values more than 353,000 real estate parcels and works on a four-year reappraisal cycle. The last reappraisal happened in 2025 and the next is set for 2029, while business personal property is appraised every year. The Assessor's page says the office estimates market value from sales, cost and income data using a computer-assisted mass appraisal system.

The state turns that value into a tax base using a fixed ratio. Houses and farms count at a quarter of appraised value, while commercial and industrial parcels count at 40 percent. For a house appraised at $250,000 the assessed value is $62,500, and the rate then multiplies every hundred dollars of it. Find the county rate on the line of your notice. For Memphis houses, the Memphis council fixes the city rate, and city levies use the Assessor's certified values dated each January 1.

When does Shelby County property tax become delinquent?

County tax opens on October 5 this year, the first Monday of the month, and runs to the end of February before turning delinquent on March 1. From that date 1.5 percent of the base tax is added monthly until the bill is cleared. Envelopes need a postmark by February's final day, and partial payments are accepted. Memphis follows a different calendar, since its tax is billed after the City Council sets the rate in mid to late June and is delinquent after August 31.

Delinquency dates and penalties by taxing body (Shelby County Trustee, Interest Rates page)

Shelby County, Arlington, Collierville, Lakeland, MillingtonMarch 11.5% a month, 18% a year

BartlettMarch 11.5% interest plus a 5% penalty in month one, then 1.5% a month

For a Memphis house, both the county bill and the city bill must be settled at a sale. Ask the Trustee and the City Treasury for separate payoffs.

Can I contest my Shelby County assessed value?

A petition goes to the Shelby County Board of Equalization, the body that examines and equalizes the Assessor's values, and filing costs nothing. The 2026 window opened May 1 and closed June 30, 2026, so it has passed for this year, and an appeal can raise, lower or leave the value unchanged. The Board's page warns that a disputed assessment generally becomes final for the year if it is not appealed on time.

Owners can file online through the Board's e-file site, by mail with a postmark by the deadline, or in person at the Board's office on weekdays The online system runs only during appeal season and accepts uploaded supporting documents. Hearing notices go out at least two weeks ahead, and the Board points out that rescheduling is generally impractical and that all documentation must be brought to the hearing. Call (901) 222-7300 with procedural questions, and watch the Board's page for the next window.

What help exists for Shelby County owners who are behind or on a fixed income?

The Trustee offers a Quarterly Payment Program for retired or unemployed residents aged 65 and over, live on a fixed income, and occupy their own home in Memphis or Shelby County with no delinquent taxes. Applicants reapply every year, and applications are available July through October 2026. Shelby County installments are due October 31, January 31, April 30 and July 31, and Memphis installments fall on August 31, November 30, February 28 and May 31.

A Written Payment Plan is a different tool for owners who are already delinquent. To qualify, the parcel must be scheduled for a current tax sale, every delinquent year must be included, the term cannot exceed 24 months, and monthly payments are due by the 20th. Call the Tax Sale Department at (901) 222-0200. For older homeowners, the City of Memphis also lists Tax Relief and Tax Freeze programs, with an income limit set by the State of Tennessee annually.

What does a Shelby County seller need to settle before closing?

The Trustee verifies every payoff on the day payment arrives, and the tax lien is not released until the balance is paid in full. A closing agent should therefore request a fresh payoff, not rely on an earlier figure. Interest is totaled through each month's end, though legal fees can be added mid-month, so a closing near the turn of a month deserves care.

State law directs the Trustee to sue for delinquent real estate tax, and Memphis turns real estate accounts over to its delinquent attorneys on February 1 once they are a full year behind. Seasonal Trustee branches operate in Bartlett, Germantown, Arlington, Collierville, Millington and Raleigh, and the Raleigh Library branch is open only on February 12 and 19, 2027. Year-round payment is at 157 Poplar Avenue, by phone at (901) 222-0200, or by mail.

More questions about Shelby County, TN Property Tax Guide

When is Shelby County property tax due?

Payment opened on Monday, October 5, and the deadline falls at the end of February. Delinquency starts March 1, when monthly interest of 1.5 percent begins to accrue on the base tax.

Does Memphis send a separate property tax bill?

Yes. Memphis bills its own tax after the City Council sets the rate, generally in mid to late June, and it is delinquent after August 31. Contact the City Treasury at 901-522-1111 for the city balance, in addition to the Trustee for the county balance.

Can I appeal my Shelby County property value now?

Not for 2026. The Board of Equalization accepted appeals from May 1 through June 30, 2026, and the online filing site only works during that season. Watch the Board's page or call (901) 222-7300 for the next window.

How often does Shelby County reappraise?

Every four years for real property. The last reappraisal was in 2025 and the next is scheduled for 2029. Personal property used in a business is appraised annually, according to the Assessor's page.

Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Shelby County taxes?

Only when the property is scheduled for a current tax sale. The plan must cover every delinquent year, last no longer than 24 months, and require payments by the 20th of each month. Call the Trustee's Tax Sale Department at (901) 222-0200.

Sumner County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Sumner County?

The Assessor of Property, John M. Hurt, sets values from Room 206 of the building at 355 N. Belvedere Drive in Gallatin (615-452-2412, open weekdays from 8:00 until 4:30). The office is on the second floor, just behind the Walmart. The Trustee, Cindy Williams, collects the tax from Room 107 in the same building (615-452-1260, on the same schedule).

Mailing changes for tax bills run through the assessor, whose edits to the roll feed the printed bills. A new owner who wants the notice mailed to a different address should call 615-452-2412 after closing.

Property tax sales are not run by either office. The assessor's FAQ sends people to the Clerk and Master for tax sale information.

What makes Sumner County's housing market different?

Sumner County lies on Tennessee's northern border, about 25 miles northeast of Nashville, and belongs to the Nashville metropolitan area. It covers 543 square miles, with the Cumberland River long the main route for trade. Gallatin holds the courthouse offices, and Hendersonville has the most people. Goodlettsville, Millersville, Mitchellville, Portland, Westmoreland and White House complete the eight cities, and several of them extend into neighboring counties.

Growth is the story here. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts show:

  • 215,538 residents in July 2025, up 9.8% from April 2020
  • 89,138 housing units, 72.0% owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied value of $393,100 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent of $1,424 and median household income of $90,301
  • 3,045 building permits in 2025, with 8.3% of residents in poverty

Schools are run by the Sumner County Board of Education, a twelve-member body with eleven elected district members and the Director of Schools. Because values here are higher than in Sullivan or Shelby, each point of tax rate matters more to a Sumner seller.

How is a Sumner County tax bill worked out?

The assessor lists four parts: appraised value, an assessment ratio set by state law, the assessed value, and the rate. Houses and farms are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value and commercial or industrial property at 40 percent. The county commission sets the county rate, and each city may add its own.

The calculation page posts these rates, each applied per hundred dollars of assessed value:

When and how do I pay Sumner County property tax?

Payment comes due the first Monday in October. A bill settled by February 28 has no interest, and March 1 begins delinquency. The Trustee accepts payment in these ways:

  • Online at tnpayments.com with Visa or Mastercard
  • By mail, with the top portion of the notice
  • In person at Room 107
  • By phone with a Visa or Mastercard
  • At local banks listed on the back of the notice

Cards cost 2.65 percent plus $1, a charge from the processing company. A taxpayer may split the bill into as many as five partial payments by check or cash, and whatever remains after February picks up interest on March 1. The paid status of a bill can be checked under the online payment link.

What is the path to contest a Sumner County valuation?

Call the assessor during the first week of May to book a hearing with the Sumner County Board of Equalization, which meets in June. An informal talk with the appraisal staff comes first and can be skipped. Compare your house with nearby sales and note any zoning or physical changes before you call.

The state's calendar sets May 20 as the date by which change notices should be mailed and exemptions applied for. A further appeal to the State Board of Equalization is due by August 1 or 45 days after the county board's notice, so for 2026 only owners with a later notice can still file. The assessor says values normally stay put between reappraisals, and the county is on a five-year cycle with the next one in 2029. Staff visit every property's exterior in between.

What relief and freeze programs does Sumner County run?

The Trustee runs the state tax relief rebate for elderly, disabled and disabled veteran owners, and a freeze for the county and some Sumner cities. Freeze applications for 2026 open in September 2026, relief applications are taken when bills go out, and the deadline is 35 days after the February payment date. Seniors 65 and over qualify on income. For disabled veterans and their widows, the programs are not income based. Everyone must requalify every year.

Appointments can be made by phone at 615-452-1260 or through the Trustee's online scheduler.

What does a house inside a Sumner County city pay?

An address inside a city limit owes the county rate plus the city rate. Using the posted figures on the same $200,000 house, a Gallatin address adds about $264.75 to the county's $711, for roughly $975.75. A Hendersonville address adds about $294.15, for roughly $1,005.15. These are illustrations of the arithmetic only, and cities may also levy special assessments, which the assessor says to ask each city about.

A rural address outside every city pays the county rate alone. That difference is worth checking on a listing, since two houses with the same appraised value can carry different bills.

Which other Sumner County deadlines can affect a seller?

The state calendar the assessor publishes lists dates that touch many owners:

  • January 1: the assessment date, when ownership and condition are fixed for the tax year
  • March 15: the deadline to apply for greenbelt
  • May 20: change notices are due out, and exemption applications are due
  • September 1: the cutoff for prorating tax on buildings moved, demolished, badly damaged or finished after January 1

Business owners get a personal property schedule by February 1 and return it by March 1. A seller who is also closing a business should ask the assessor whether the January 1 tangible property still shows on the roll.

What should a Sumner County seller do about the tax bill at closing?

Ask the Trustee in Room 107 for the balance on the parcel and have the title company prorate it on the settlement statement. The assessment date is January 1, so the roll shows the owner from that date. A buyer who sees no bill should phone the Trustee and update the mailing address with the assessor.

The assessor's page shows $1.421 per $100 of assessed value for the county. Gallatin adds $0.5295 and Hendersonville $0.5883 on its listing.

When is the next Sumner County reappraisal?

2029. The assessor says the county is on a five-year reappraisal cycle.

Can I pay Sumner County property tax by card?

Yes. The Trustee takes Visa and Mastercard online or by phone. The fee is 2.65 percent plus $1 and goes to the processing company.

How do I appeal my Sumner County assessment?

Call the assessor at 615-452-2412 in the first week of May to schedule a hearing before the county board, which meets in June. Gather comparable sales first.

Does Sumner County have a tax freeze?

Yes. The Trustee administers a freeze for the county and part of its cities for owners 65 or older, and applications for 2026 began in September.

Blount County by the numbers

Which Blount County offices handle property tax?

Three bodies split the work. The Property Assessor values every parcel, the Blount County Board of Commissioners sets the tax rate, and the Trustee collects the money. The Assessor's office is at 351 Court Street in the Blount County Courthouse, Maryville, TN 37804, phone 865-273-5850, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Trustee is on the third floor of the courthouse at 347 Court Street, phone 865-273-5900, with the same hours.

The county's assessor page says the office must appraise and assess about 70,000 parcels and audit at least 10 percent of business personal property accounts each year. It also makes the point that the assessor does not raise or lower taxes, since the amount owed comes from the assessed value multiplied by the tax rate. The Trustee's property tax page adds that the Trustee does not set rates or appraisals and only collects.

Blount County includes the cities of Maryville, Alcoa, Townsend, Friendsville and Rockford, plus the town of Louisville and part of Vonore. The county page covers county tax. A city may bill its own tax, and the Tennessee Comptroller notes that a city collector can be the city treasurer, the city recorder or the county trustee, so ask the city about any separate bill.

What is Blount County like, and why does it matter for a tax bill?

Blount County covers 567 square miles in East Tennessee, with Maryville as the county seat and largest city. The southern part rises into the Great Smoky Mountains, where the crest forms the border with North Carolina and Thunderhead Mountain reaches 5,527 feet. The northern part is Ridge-and-Valley country, and the Tennessee River forms part of the line with Knox County through Fort Loudoun Lake. Cades Cove is one of the most visited sections of the national park.

Schools affect where a home sits in the county's market. Blount County Schools serves the county except inside the cities of Maryville and Alcoa, which run their own school systems. Maryville College, founded in 1819, is downtown, and Denso Manufacturing Tennessee is the county's largest employer, with about 3,000 workers.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Blount County:

  • 143,820 residents in July 2025, up 6.3% from April 2020
  • 64,682 housing units, with 77.0% owner-occupied
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes of $320,500 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $77,365 and 9.2% of people in poverty
  • 790 building permits in 2025

How is a Blount County property tax bill calculated?

The bill equals the appraised value, times the assessment percentage for the property type, times the tax rate per $100 of assessed value. The assessor page lists the percentages:

  • Residential improvements and residential land: 25 percent of fair market value (land may be assessed on market value or use value)
  • Commercial property: 40 percent of fair market value
  • Personal property of commercial businesses: 30 percent of the appraised value reported on the Tangible Personal Property Schedule

The county's own example uses a $250,000 residential property. At 25 percent the assessment is $62,500, and at the 2026 rate of $1.29 per $100 the county tax bill is $806. Rates for earlier years were $2.47 per $100 from 2015 through 2022, $1.59 from 2023 through 2025, and $1.29 for 2026.

The Trustee reports where the money goes: 46.50 percent to general county purposes, 42.65 percent to education and 10.85 percent to debt, with over 95 percent of that debt tied to education. Property tax is about 40 percent of the funds the Trustee collects, and State of Tennessee money, mainly for education, is another 30 percent.

When is Blount County property tax due, and what discount applies now?

County notices are typically mailed in early to mid-September and payable through the end of February. Taxes become delinquent on March 1, and state law adds 1.5 percent interest per month to delinquent property tax until it is paid. The county gives a 2 percent discount for payment by the end of October and 1 percent during November. Today is November 15, 2026, so the 1 percent discount is still open through November 30 and the 2 percent discount has ended.

State law does not require a notice, and the county sends one as a reminder. An owner who has not received one by October 1 should call the Trustee. Payment options include:

  • In person or by mail at 347 Court Street, Maryville
  • Online by card or e-check, and by phone at 855-777-3468, with a convenience fee that goes to the payment vendors and not to the county
  • Most Blount County banks until the delinquency date, with the tax notice in hand, though state law does not allow payment at credit unions

How do I appeal a Blount County assessment?

Start with the County Board of Equalization, which meets June 1. A disputed assessment must first go to the county board or it becomes final, with limited exceptions. Some assessors offer an informal review, which can speed a correction, though it does not count as an appeal. Contact the Assessor at 865-273-5850 to ask whether Blount County does and how to get on the county board's schedule.

An owner who disagrees with the county board's decision can appeal to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 of the tax year or within 45 days of the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. For tax year 2026 the August 1 date has passed, so an owner with a later notice should call the State Board at 615-401-7883 to check the 45-day window. The state hearing is held before an administrative judge, who must issue a ruling within 90 days. The taxpayer carries the burden of proof.

The state's guidance points to evidence that works:

  • Sales of comparable properties, with differences in size, age, condition and location explained
  • An appraisal, which may be presented and may require the appraiser to testify
  • A statement of the value the owner claims, since a bare claim of overvaluation is generally not enough

Pay at least the undisputed part of the bill before it goes delinquent. Any delinquent taxes from earlier years must be paid in full as well, and the Comptroller's appeal page explains how to work out the undisputed amount. A higher value after a countywide reappraisal does not by itself show the assessment is wrong.

What tax relief and freeze programs does Blount County offer?

Two state programs run through the Trustee's office. The Property Tax Relief Program is a rebate for homeowners 65 or older whose combined income from all sources for all owners, spouse included, is not over $38,470, using 2025 income for the 2026 tax year. It can also reach totally and permanently disabled taxpayers with the same income limit, certain service-connected disabled veterans and certain widows of those veterans.

The Property Tax Freeze Program lets owners 65 or older by the end of the tax year freeze all or part of their county tax. They must be the owners on the recorded deed, live in the home as a principal residence and have 2025 combined income of no more than $63,470. State law limits how much land qualifies, so a 100-acre farm would freeze only the residence and part of its land. Owners must apply and be approved every year.

The deadline for both programs for the 2026 tax year is April 5, 2027. Call 865-273-5900 to learn what documents are needed.

What happens to property tax when a Blount County house is sold?

The official tax roll reflects ownership on January 1, so the name on the 2026 bill may be the seller's even after a fall closing. The Trustee says taxes are normally prorated at closing and the buyer becomes responsible, and that its office tries to send the notice to the new owner but does not always know who agreed to pay. A buyer who gets no notice should call the Trustee and ask for the status of the parcel.

A seller who owes back tax should check the amount with the Trustee early. Interest of 1.5 percent a month runs on delinquent taxes. A seller who needs a quick closing and has an unpaid balance, a pending appeal or an estate to settle can ask the title company how those items will be handled at the table.

More questions about Blount County, TN Property Tax Guide

What is the Blount County property tax rate for 2026?

The 2026 county rate is $1.29 per $100 of assessed value, set by the Blount County Board of Commissioners. On a $250,000 home assessed at 25 percent, the county's example works out to $806. Any city tax would be separate.

When are Blount County property taxes delinquent?

They become delinquent on March 1, after the payment period that runs through the end of February. State law adds 1.5 percent interest each month to delinquent property tax. The 2026 deadline for relief and freeze applications is April 5, 2027.

Is there still a discount for paying Blount County property tax early?

Yes, for a short time. The 2 percent discount ended with October, and the 1 percent discount applies to payments made during November. Discounts are shown on the tax notice and are not available after those periods.

Where do I pay property tax in Blount County?

Pay the Trustee at 347 Court Street, Maryville, by mail, online, or by phone at 855-777-3468. Most Blount County banks accept payment until the delinquency date, but credit unions cannot take payments under state law. Card and e-check payments carry a convenience fee.

How do I challenge my Blount County property value?

File a complaint with the County Board of Equalization, which meets June 1, then appeal to the State Board of Equalization if needed. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal. Pay at least the undisputed part of the tax so the bill is not treated as delinquent.

Hamilton County by the numbers

What sets Hamilton County apart for a home seller?

Hamilton County is the metro heart of southeast Tennessee. The Tennessee River winds through Chattanooga, the county seat, and the Georgia line forms the southern edge. Only a few counties in the country share a boundary with ten others, and this is one. The General Assembly created it on October 25, 1819, and by the 2020 count it was fourth in the state for population. Lookout Mountain with Point Park and Ruby Falls draws visitors, and Interstates 24 and 75 are the main arteries.

Beyond Chattanooga, the county holds Collegedale, East Ridge, Lakesite, Red Bank, Ridgeside and Soddy-Daisy as cities, plus the towns of Lookout Mountain, Signal Mountain and Walden. Who collects your tax and at what rate depends on which of these your address falls in.

Census QuickFacts puts numbers on the county:

  • 390,833 people in July 2025, 6.5 percent more than in April 2020
  • 176,983 homes and apartments, with 63.9 percent occupied by owners
  • $312,800 as the middle value of an owner's home in the 2020 to 2024 survey period
  • $76,183 as household income, and 37.5 percent of adults holding a bachelor's degree or more
  • 1,887 building permits in 2025

Compare that $312,800 with $207,500 in Greene County and $210,900 in Hamblen County, and you can see why a tax bill here weighs more.

Who bills and who collects property tax in Hamilton County?

One office values, one body sets the rate, and one office collects. The Assessor of Property appraises, the Board of Commissioners picks the county rate, and the Trustee sends bills and takes payment. The Trustee sits in Room 210 of the courthouse on Georgia Avenue in Chattanooga and runs a second counter at 6125 Preservation Drive, Suite 101, in the Bonny Oaks Industrial Park. Both open from eight to four on weekdays. Call (423) 209-7270.

The Trustee also bills for Collegedale, East Ridge, Lakesite, Red Bank, Ridgeside, Soddy Daisy and Walden. Chattanooga does its own billing through the City Treasurer at City Hall, 101 E 11th Street, Room 100. That office answers at (423) 643-7262 or ptax@chattanooga.gov. A house in Chattanooga therefore gets two separate bills.

Marty Haynes is the Assessor of Property, at 6135 Heritage Park Drive, (423) 209-7300. His office's FAQ points out that it only sets values. When a bill goes up and the value did not move, the cause is a higher rate.

What is the Hamilton County property tax rate?

On June 3, 2025 the county mayor and the assessor announced a certified rate of $1.51 per $100 of assessed value, replacing $2.23. They described it as the lowest since 1941 and said it followed the four-year reappraisal. It went on the bills mailed in fall 2025. The assessor estimated that roughly two thirds of owners would pay the same or less county tax than they did in 2024. Their release adds that state law forces a lower certified rate after a reappraisal so that rising values do not create a windfall, although local governments may raise it again.

Chattanooga's tax page lists a separate city rate of 1.93 per $100. Houses count at one quarter of appraised value for tax purposes, and commercial buildings at two fifths. So a Chattanooga home appraised at $312,800 has an assessed value of $78,200. Divide that by 100, then multiply by the county rate and again by the city rate to see the two bills. Phone the Trustee to learn the rate printed on this year's notice.

When are Hamilton County taxes due and what is the penalty for paying late?

Notices go out in late September, and the payment window opens October 1 and stays open through the last day of February. In mid-November 2026 the window is open and no interest has built up. Starting March 1, the county adds 1.5 percent a month, which it describes as 18 percent a year.

The Trustee's FAQ gives practical rules:

  • You may pay in part, and the office accepts partial payments
  • For mailed checks, only a postmark by the deadline counts, and the office's own meter stamps are rejected
  • Online payments are treated as made on the day of the transaction
  • Any First Horizon Bank in the county will take a current-year payment if you bring the original bill

No state rule makes the county mail a notice, and the Trustee says a missing one does not erase interest. Chattanooga uses a different late schedule, charging 1 percent interest and a half percent penalty each month, and it hands unpaid earlier years to the Chancery Court in March. Taxes that stay unpaid can end up at the county's June tax sale, which carries a one year redemption period.

How can I challenge my Hamilton County property value?

Talk to the appraisers first. Look up your parcel on the Assessor's property search and sales comparison tools, or ring 423-209-7990 to discuss it with a staff appraiser. The Assessor wants informal review requests in before May 20.

Still unhappy? Ask the Assessor's office for the form to appear before the county Board of Equalization. That board meets during June and takes filings into the first week of the month, so confirm the closing date by phone. A later stage is the State Board of Equalization, where an administrative judge hears the case. The owner has to prove the number, and the state says matched sales of similar homes make the strongest evidence.

Hamilton County revalues on a four-year cycle. The latest round took effect in 2025, and the next one is set for 2029. In the years between, the Comptroller's schedule still lets an assessor fix mistakes in ownership, location or physical description when the owner asks before March 1.

What relief programs apply to Hamilton County owners?

Tennessee refunds a slice of the tax to low-income seniors, disabled homeowners and disabled veterans. The county's FAQ quotes a $37,530 income ceiling for 2025. The state's 2026 brochure raises that to $38,470 of 2025 income, with a $33,600 value cap for seniors and disabled owners and $175,000 for veterans. Hamilton County says it matches what the state pays. To book a time, call the Bonny Oaks office at (423) 209-7799.

The freeze for owners 65 and older follows different lines. The county government is missing from the Comptroller's list of 28 freeze counties, yet Chattanooga adopted one in 2017 and uses a 2026 income limit of $63,470. It reduces only the city bill. For land used for farming or forestry, the Assessor runs the Greenbelt program, which requires 15 acres or more.

How does the property tax bill work when I sell in Hamilton County?

Bills are addressed to the owner of record. The Trustee advises new owners to read their closing statement or call the title company, since what each person owes turns on the transfer date, and an unpaid balance stays with the parcel. Before you list, ask the Trustee's office for the balance on each tax year, plus any city balance if the house is in Chattanooga.

If you inherited the home or fell behind, the title company can pay what you owe from your proceeds at the closing table. The Register of Deeds, reachable at (423) 209-6560, records the deed and collects the state transfer tax.

What is the Hamilton County property tax rate?

The county's certified rate for 2025 was $1.51 per $100 of assessed value, replacing $2.23. Chattanooga's page shows its own city rate of 1.93 per $100. Call the Trustee at (423) 209-7270 to confirm what your bill uses.

When are Hamilton County property taxes due?

From October 1 through the last day of February. Interest of 1.5 percent a month starts March 1. Notices go out near the end of September, though state law does not demand them.

How often does Hamilton County reappraise property?

Every four years. According to the Assessor's FAQ, the last reappraisal was in 2025 and the next comes in 2029. Between reappraisals, a record error can still be corrected on request.

Do I pay both Chattanooga and Hamilton County property tax?

Yes, a Chattanooga owner gets a county bill from the Trustee and a separate city bill from the City Treasurer. The Trustee also collects for seven other cities, among them East Ridge and Soddy Daisy.

Is there property tax relief for seniors in Hamilton County?

Yes. The state reimburses owners 65 or older whose income is under the limit, and the county matches the state amount. Chattanooga adds a freeze for seniors. Call (423) 209-7799 for an appointment.

Sullivan County fills the northeast corner of Tennessee along the Virginia line. It was cut from Washington County in 1779 and covers 430 square miles, of which 413 are land. Kingsport has the most residents, and Bristol, Bluff City and a slice of Johnson City also fall inside. Blountville, the county seat, is the only unincorporated county seat in Tennessee.

The land runs from Ridge-and-Valley ridges in the west to the Blue Ridge in the east, where Holston Mountain tops out at 4,284 feet. For tax year 2026 the August date has passed, so an owner holding a later notice should call 615-401-7883 to check the 45-day window.

The state's guidance says the best proof for a house is sales of comparable homes, with differences in size, age, condition and location explained. An appraisal may also be offered. A statement that a house is overvalued, with no figure behind it, is usually not enough. The taxpayer must still pay the undisputed part of the bill on time, along with any older delinquent tax.

What tax relief is there for Sullivan County homeowners?

The state relief rebate covers owners who live in their home and are 65 or older, disabled, or a qualifying disabled veteran or widow of one. Elderly and disabled applicants may have combined household income of no more than $38,470, spouse included. Bring proof of income, a Social Security card and proof of residency and age. Call 423-323-6470 or 423-323-6469 for an appointment.

The signed voucher must come back to a Trustee office each year by April 5, and bank branches do not accept it. Sullivan County does not offer a tax freeze program.

Can a Sullivan County owner qualify for greenbelt or an exemption?

The Assessor's office also manages Greenbelt and Forestry assessments. The state calendar sets March 15 as the greenbelt application deadline and May 20 for exemption applications. An owner of acreage should call the Assessor about both programs before listing.

Anyone who owns a business furnishing or equipment on January 1 may owe personal property tax even after closing the shop. The Trustee says the business must be formally closed with the right agencies.

Who pays the tax when a Sullivan County house sells?

Whoever held title on January 1 gets the notice, even when the house changes hands later in the year. The Trustee says new owners still must see that the tax is paid on time, and to follow the settlement statement for the split. If a lender escrows the taxes, the mortgage company gets the bill.

A seller with unpaid tax should settle the balance with the Trustee before closing. Interest can be removed only by a court order or an assessment change from the State Board or the Assessor, so a late bill rarely gets waived.

No discount is listed. Taxes can be paid without penalty from October 1 through February 28, and the Trustee permits installments in that window.

Pay at the Trustee in Blountville, or at the seasonal Bristol and Kingsport counters from October 1 through March 15. Bank of Tennessee branches also take cash or check payments with the notice.

The Assessor's page lists 2027 as the next county-wide reappraisal. The Assessor's 2025 update described a reappraisal that year, with revaluation notices going out in the spring.

Which Williamson County office sends the bill, and which one sets the value?

Trustee Karen Paris sits in Suite 203 at 1320 West Main Street in Franklin (zip 37064). Her number is 615-790-5709, and the front counter keeps weekday hours from 8:00 until 4:30. Value or address-change calls go to the Assessor, 615-790-5708.

Who the Trustee bills for is spelled out in the county's own pages: Williamson County itself, the Franklin Special School District, Brentwood, Franklin, Nolensville and Thompson's Station. The rate page sends Spring Hill and Fairview residents to their city governments, so owners in those two towns should phone city hall to learn which office handles their city bill.

Forgiveness is off the table. The Trustee's FAQ cites T.C.A. 67-5-2803 for the point that the office cannot waive, prorate or release any part of the tax or its interest.

What is Williamson County like, and why are values here so high?

Williamson County is a Middle Tennessee county that touches Davidson County, with Franklin as its seat of government. Lawmakers carved it from Davidson County on October 26, 1799. Abram Maury platted Franklin the following year. It spans roughly 584 square miles, drained mainly by the Harpeth River and the Little Harpeth River, and the Natchez Trace Parkway crosses it.

Old buildings shape the market. Franklin saw one of the war's bloodiest battles, and 1,481 soldiers lie in the McGavock Confederate Cemetery. A former stove factory in town was converted to offices, shops, restaurants and event rooms. Since the interstates came through, people poured in: the 2020 census counted 247,726 residents, a jump of 35.2 percent from 2010 and the biggest gain the county has recorded. Brentwood and Franklin anchor the north, and the south end keeps its farm character. Williamson County Schools covers most of the county, while part of Franklin sends kindergarten through eighth graders to the Franklin Special School District.

  • 272,061 people as of July 2025, up 9.8% since the April 2020 base

  • A typical owned home worth $751,900, about three times the figure in Washington County or Tipton County
  • Household income near $135,594, and 62.7% of adults 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree or more
  • 1,621 building permits issued in 2025

How is Williamson County property tax figured?

The state sets the ratios: 25 percent of appraised value for a home, 40 percent for commercial and industrial, 30 percent for business personal property. The rate is then applied to each $100 of the assessed figure. At a $751,900 home, the Census median, the assessed value would be $187,975, so every $1.00 of rate per $100 would add about $1,880 to the bill.

The county posts its 2026 rates as a chart on its Property Tax Rates page, and the county rate has to be combined with the city or school district that applies to the address. Brentwood, Franklin, Nolensville, Thompson's Station and the Franklin Special School District are billed through the Trustee. The Assessor values new construction up to September 1, and then the rolls pass to the Trustee.

The roll is open to the public in May, and owners whose value changed get a notice by mail. Reading the roll early lets an owner act before the June hearing window.

How long does a Williamson County owner have to pay without interest?

Mailing happens in early October. From the first Monday that month through the final day of February, the bill can be settled with no added charge, including in installments. Beginning March 1, the Trustee adds 1.5 percent, then adds it again at the start of every following month. One bill covers a single calendar year. With today at November 15, 2026, the 2026 bill has not started to accrue anything.

When a lender pays the tax from escrow, the owner still gets a statement, which the Trustee calls a copy for the owner's records. Ask the Trustee's office which payment methods it takes for the 2026 bill.

  • Nobody at the counter can erase interest, because the law gives the Trustee no such power

How does a Williamson County owner contest a valuation?

The first call is to the Assessor at 615-790-5708, to walk through how the value was reached. The county notes that many disputes end right there. Even so, an owner has to book a hearing slot with the county's equalization board to keep appeal rights intact. Five residents sit on that board, each named by the County Commission to a two-year term. It hears cases in June, and the Assessor's staff ask owners to phone during the first week of June. Only the person on the roll, an authorized agent or the owner can file.

The next stop after a county hearing is the State Board of Equalization. It accepts filings until August 1 of the tax year, or until 45 days after the county notice if that date is later, and its administrative judge issues a decision within 90 days of the hearing. The state calls sales of comparable properties the best proof for a house and says an unsupported claim of overvaluation rarely works. Settle the undisputed part of the tax before March 1.

What tax relief and freeze programs does Williamson County offer?

The Trustee administers four programs, two of them state-funded, and appointments are required. Disabled veterans and their widows or widowers have a separate state program, so call for the paperwork it needs. Each looks at 2025 income from every source for the applicant, spouse and co-owners, and the elderly programs require the applicant to reach 65 by the end of 2026. Applications for 2026 relief are taken after the 2026 bill arrives and until April 5, 2027, with the tax paid in full first. The freeze fixes the home's tax at the qualifying year's amount for as long as the owner re-qualifies every year. It covers the residence and up to 5 acres, and the base resets if improvements raise the value or the owner buys another home. Call 615-790-5709 to book.

What happens to the tax when a Williamson County house changes hands?

Because the January 1 owner receives the statement, a seller who closes in the fall still gets the 2026 mailing and has to pass it along. Ask the title company how the year will be divided in the settlement. A seller who is enrolled in the freeze should talk to the Trustee first, because selling and then buying another home resets the base amount.

February 28 is the last interest-free day, and the 1.5 percent monthly charge begins March 1.

No. State law leaves the Trustee without authority to waive, prorate or release any of the tax or its interest.

The limit for tax year 2026 is $69,150 of combined 2025 income across the applicant, spouse and co-owners, and the applicant must turn 65 by December 31, 2026.

The Property Assessor's line is 615-790-5708. To reach the county equalization board, call that office during the first week of June.

Who handles property tax in Wilson County, Tennessee?

Two county offices share the work: the Property Assessor sets values, and the Trustee sends and collects the bills. Both sit in the Wilson County Courthouse area of downtown Lebanon, at 228 East Main Street.

The Trustee, Kenneth Hackett, is in Room 102 (mailing address P.O. Box 865, Lebanon, TN 37088) and answers at 615-444-0894. One practical point: mailing address changes for tax bills go through the Assessor, not the Trustee, using a change of address form or a phone call.

What is Wilson County like for a home seller?

Wilson County lies in Middle Tennessee, east of Nashville, and covers about 583 square miles including roughly 12 square miles of water. The General Assembly created it in 1799 from part of Sumner County. Lebanon is the county seat, Mt. Juliet is the largest city, and Watertown is the county's town.

The Cumberland River forms the northern edge as Old Hickory Lake, and several western streams belong to the Stones River basin. The county also holds a large concentration of cedar glades, many inside Cedars of Lebanon State Park. Interstate 40 and Interstate 840 cross it, along with US 70 and US 231.

The 2020 census counted 147,737 people and 58,152 housing units, and 75.1% of occupied homes were owner occupied. The 2025 estimate is 175,033, so assessments here reflect fast growth. Tax notices go out in mid-October to the property address. The tax year runs January 1 through December 31, and the bill can be paid without interest from mid-October through the last day of February of the following year.

Owners may appear themselves or send a family member, attorney or authorized agent, and should arrive about fifteen minutes early to fill out a form.

The board looks only at fair and equitable value. Evidence about how much tax you can afford does not help. Results are normally mailed before the end of June, and the decision letter explains how to go to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 or 45 days after the letter, whichever is later.

  • Tell the title company which tax year is unpaid so it can collect from your proceeds.

Business tangible personal property is a separate account. If a home business operated from the property, the schedule is due to the Assessor by March 1 each year, and the county places a forced assessment when none is filed.

Call or visit the Assessor at 615-444-8661 first. If that does not settle it, request a hearing before the County Board of Equalization, which starts meeting June 1. A State Board of Equalization appeal is due by August 1 or 45 days after the county letter.

With prices climbing across the county, an owner whose house was last valued before the recent run-up should look at the new notice closely.

The formula is short. Multiply the appraised value by the assessment ratio for the property's class, then apply the rate to every $100 of the result. Since August 1, 2026 has passed, an owner holding a late county notice should count forward from the mailing date. An administrative judge hears the case and rules no more than 90 days after the hearing, and court review has to be sought inside 60 days once the state board's order is final.

Some assessors offer an informal review that can speed a correction. It is no appeal and protects nothing later, so ask whether the Maury office offers one and still file with the county board to keep every option.

Yes. The Trustee's office helps elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans apply for the Tennessee Tax Relief Program under state guidelines. Call 931-375-2201 for the forms and the current income limits.

The Trustee also offers ACH debits that can spread the bill into equal monthly payments. Call 931-375-2201 to ask how to enroll.

How does a sale change who pays Maury County tax?

The tax year runs on the calendar, and the notice goes to whoever owned the house on January 1. A sale in the fall therefore leaves the seller's name on the bill even though the buyer will carry the house into the next year. Request the Trustee's exact balance and let the title agent split it at closing.

Late sellers face a short clock, because charges start in March and the Chancery Court turnover follows in April. Any balance still open at closing comes out of the seller's net, so confirm the amount with the Trustee a week ahead.

Yes. The Assessor's page says reappraisals run every four years and that 2026 is the current reappraisal year. Values come from market prices as of January 1 of that year.

On March 1. Interest of 1.5 percent a month starts then and climbs each month, and on April 1 the county turns delinquent accounts over to Chancery Court. Payment is open from the first Monday in October through February.

Yes, the Trustee accepts them. Interest still applies on March 1 to any balance left unpaid, so a partial payment lowers the amount that accrues interest without ending it.

Which offices handle property tax in Sevier County?

Three offices split the job, and all of them work out of the Sevier County Courthouse at 125 Court Avenue in Sevierville. One values the land and buildings, the County Commission chooses the rate, and the Trustee prints the bills and collects. Knowing which desk answers which question saves walking between floors.

What should a seller know about Sevier County itself?

Sevier County spreads over 598 square miles along the northern edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, and Sevierville anchors it as the seat of government. Roughly thirty percent of the national park falls inside the county lines, and visitor spending drives the local economy. Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge offer Ripley's Aquarium of the Smokies, Ober Gatlinburg and Dollywood, and cabin rentals have multiplied alongside them. The Assessor runs an online filing for nightly rentals, and the county posts a short-term rental tax estimator beside its primary home and vacant land estimator. Census Bureau QuickFacts for Sevier County reports:

How is a Sevier County property tax bill figured?

Tennessee takes the appraised value, applies a ratio fixed by state law, and multiplies the result by the local rate. The State Comptroller's tax bill guide puts residential and farm land at one quarter of appraised value and commercial or industrial land at 40 percent. Rates are stated for each hundred dollars of assessed value.

Take a house appraised at $300,000. Its assessed value is $75,000. Using the $1.48 listed in the Trustee's FAQ for 2024, the yearly tax would be $1,110. That is only an illustration, because Sevier County reappraises on a five-year cycle and 2026 is a reappraisal year. The county's statement on reappraisal notices says the Assessor must review roughly 90,000 parcels, a certified rate is then calculated under state law to hold total collections steady, and the Board of Commissioners adopts the final figure. Some owners will see higher bills and some lower, so read the 2026 bill itself.

Between cycles, values stay where they are unless the property physically changes. A change in ownership alone does not move the assessment.

The 2026 bills were mailed in early October and can be paid from October 1 onward without penalty, through the end of February 2027. This mid-November week falls inside that window. After the deadline, interest of 1.5 percent accrues every month on the unpaid base amount. Checks sent by mail must carry a postmark dated no later than that last day, since the Trustee refuses office meter dates, and card or e-check payments count on the day of the transaction. Partial payments are welcome, and only the leftover balance collects interest.

How do I dispute a Sevier County assessment?

Call the Assessor first, then carry the dispute to the Board of Equalization if the answer falls short.   • Tax Freeze, age 65 and up: income may not exceed $47,990 for 2024, and the application is renewed each year

Relief reaches city taxes too. Greenbelt is a separate break for parcels of 15 acres or more in farm or forestry use, requested by March 1; land that drops out owes a rollback of the taxes saved over the last three years. Ask the Trustee for the limits that apply this year before you plan around these figures.

What happens to unpaid Sevier County tax when I sell?

The tax lien follows the parcel, so any balance must be cleared at or before closing. The Trustee mails each bill to whoever is listed as owner, and its FAQ tells new buyers to read the closing statement to learn who handles that year's tax. The title company ordinarily settles any open balance at the table.

If a bill is not paid by the deadline, the account turns delinquent and moves to Chancery Court, where costs are added and the parcel can be advertised for the yearly auction. The Clerk and Master publishes the list 20 to 30 days ahead, bidders register in person half an hour before the sale starts, and payment is cash, money order or check. The former owner has a year to redeem, and the bidder earns 1 percent per month in the meantime. Anyone with a delinquent account should phone the Trustee at (865) 453-2767 before the list appears.

The final day of February. For the 2026 bill, that is February 2027. Beginning March 1, interest runs at 1.5 percent monthly (18 percent yearly), and a late postmark counts as a late payment.

Every five years, with 2026 as the current reappraisal year. The Assessor's page explains that values hold between cycles unless the property physically changes. After reappraisal, a certified rate is calculated so total collections stay steady.

It will not stop the sale, but the balance has to come from sale money because the lien stays on the parcel. Ask the Trustee what the exact payoff is on your closing date. Accounts sent to Chancery Court pick up costs and can end in a tax sale.

  • A specific figure you propose, supported by facts about the house

You must also pay the part of the bill you do not dispute and any older unpaid years by the delinquency date.

Does Hamblen County have a tax freeze or relief?

It has both. The state relief program refunds part of the tax for low-income seniors, disabled owners and some veterans. Applications go to the Trustee, who must receive them within 35 days of the delinquency date.

Hamblen is on the Comptroller's list of 28 counties with a freeze. It joined in 2007, and the 2026 income limit is $39,260. An owner who turns 65 by year end and meets the income test can fix the tax on a main home at the first qualifying year's amount. Each year requires a new application, and the fixed amount grows if the owner improves the property or moves to a different house.

What should I do about Hamblen County tax before I sell?

The Assessor's record date is January 1, but the title company splits the year's bill between buyer and seller at the table. Get the balance from the Trustee before listing, most of all for an inherited house or one with several unpaid years, because interest begins accruing once March 1 passes.

On its website the Clerk and Master, at 423-586-9112, keeps a delinquent tax section along with a tax search and payment tool. Once the sale closes, the deed is recorded in the Register of Deeds office inside the same courthouse, which also collects the state's recording taxes.

The Assessor supplies the assessed value, the County Commission sets the rate, and the Trustee multiplies the two to produce the bill. The Trustee's page includes a tax calculator if you want to test a figure before the bills arrive.

Hawkins County's commission has 14 members, two from each of seven civil districts, and it adopts the rate along with the annual budget for the general, school and highway funds. What is Hawkins County like for homeowners and sellers?

Hawkins County covers about 500 square miles in the northeast corner of Tennessee, with Rogersville as the county seat and its 1836 courthouse the oldest in the state. Church Hill is the largest city. Bulls Gap, Mount Carmel and Surgoinsville are towns, and Bean Station and Kingsport reach into the county.

The Census Bureau estimates 59,559 residents for 2025 and about 28,006 housing units. For 2020-2024 it reports 80.1% owner-occupied homes, a median owner-occupied value of $176,300, median gross rent of $785 and a median household income of $56,936.   • The county government does not issue building permits and has no zoning restrictions or code enforcement, according to the county home page. Permits come through the State of Tennessee.

Who sends and who sets a Washington County tax bill?

The Assessor of Property values the land and buildings, the County Commission picks the rate, and the Trustee collects. The Trustee's page is blunt about it: the Trustee only collects, and has no role in appraisals or in setting the rate. Value questions go to the Assessor at 423-753-1671.

The Trustee, Rick Storey, runs two counters. The Jonesborough office is in the Historic Courthouse downtown, phone 423-753-1602, open weekdays 8 to 4:30, with a drop box at the corner of the courthouse. The Johnson City office is at 378 Marketplace Boulevard, phone 423-610-7211, with hours of 8:30 to 4:30 listed from November 3, 2025. Mail goes to PO Box 215, Jonesborough, TN 37659.

The county bill does not cover everything. The Trustee notes that homes in Johnson City or the Town of Jonesborough also owe city property tax, so a house inside either one gets more than one bill.

What is Washington County like, and how does that show up in values?

Washington County is the oldest county in Tennessee, set up in 1777 while the area still belonged to North Carolina. Jonesborough, the seat of government, is called Tennessee's oldest town. Johnson City, the largest city, started as a railroad depot and is now home to East Tennessee State University and a regional medical center. The county covers 330 square miles, with the Nolichucky River crossing the south and the Watauga River along the north.

Ridges and valleys fill the west, while the Blue Ridge side rises in the east toward Buffalo Mountain and the Cherokee National Forest. Interstates 26 and 81 both cross the county. Two public school systems serve it: Washington County Schools, and Johnson City Schools for most of that city. Gray, Telford, Fall Branch and Oak Grove are census-designated places outside the two main towns.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table for the county shows:

  • 141,199 people as of July 2025, a 6.2% gain on the April 2020 count

One local wrinkle: after the Hurricane Helene flooding of 2024, the Assessor's office asked affected owners to return a reassessment form so values could be adjusted.

How does Washington County calculate the tax on a house?

The Trustee spells out three steps: take the appraised value, multiply by 25 percent for residential property (40 percent for commercial), then multiply the result by the rate for each $100. The county's example is a $150,000 home, which becomes $37,500 of assessed value and a bill of $806.25. Since tax year 2020 the County Commission rounds bills to the nearest dollar, so that example reads $806.

The Trustee's page shows $2.15 for each $100, labeled as the 2023 county rate. Run on a home at the Census median of $249,000, the county tax would be about $1,338 a year at that rate. Confirm the current figure with the Trustee before relying on it. The rate splits among these funds:

When is Washington County property tax due, and what if the notice never arrives?

Notices usually go out in October and the tax is payable through the end of February. A balance still open on March 1 gets 1.5 percent interest, added each month. The Trustee wants taxes paid on time whether or not a notice shows up, and asks anyone who has not received one by November 15 to call. That date is today, so an owner without a bill, other than a mortgage escrow customer, should phone 423-753-1602 now.

  • Online at washington.paytntaxes.com, entering the tax year and bill number
  • By phone at 1-855-777-3468, or by e-check from a personal account

The Trustee also allows partial and prepaid payments, handled at the two offices. A 2021 notice from the office said unpaid balances after the delinquency period move to the Clerk and Master for collection, so ask the Trustee how that date works for the current year before letting a bill slide.

What can a Washington County owner do about a value that looks too high?

Each May the Assessor opens the assessment roll for viewing and mails notice to owners whose values changed. An owner who thinks the figure is above market value can take it to the county's Board of Equalization, which hears the case and finalizes the roll. Call 423-753-1671 to ask about the board's schedule and to request an informal look at the value.

Nashville backs up the local board. A losing owner can carry the dispute to the state level, with a filing window that closes on August 1 or 45 days after the county's notice was mailed, whichever comes later. Pay the undisputed share of the bill on time while waiting. The state's guidance leans on sales of similar homes, a professional appraisal and a clearly stated value, and the owner has to prove the case before an administrative judge.

What tax relief programs apply in Washington County?

The state Tax Relief Program began in 1973 and reimburses qualified elderly and disabled homeowners, as well as disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. The Trustee says Washington County matches the state amount, up to the amount billed. A veteran rated 100 percent disabled qualifies, and the relief passes to a surviving spouse. Relief is not an exemption, so the bill is paid first.

Applicants bring a driver's license, Medicare card, Social Security card and proof of the previous year's income. The state sends the income threshold to the Trustee in November. Other counties list the 2026 cap as $38,470 on 2025 income, so ask the Trustee in Washington County to confirm. A voucher has to be returned each year or the relief lapses for that year.

How does a Washington County sale change who owes the tax?

State law fixes the official tax roll as of January 1, so whoever is on the roll that day is the owner of record for the year. After a sale the Trustee tries to mail a notice to the buyer, since the office cannot know who agreed to pay. Taxes are normally prorated at closing and the buyer is made the responsible party. A buyer who gets no notice is asked to call and check the parcel.

A seller carrying an unpaid balance can ask the Trustee for the exact payoff with interest, and the title company then puts that figure on the settlement statement. Things to line up before a sale:

Which offices bill and value property in Montgomery County?

County commissioners adopt the rate, and the Trustee applies it per $100 of assessed value. A house within Clarksville limits gets a second bill from the City of Clarksville, so a seller there clears two balances.

What kind of county is Montgomery County for a seller?

The county was formed in 1796. Clarksville is its seat and its single incorporated municipality, and the county belongs to the Clarksville, TN-KY metro area. QuickFacts shows 249,935 residents in July 2025, up 13.6% from 220,012 at the 2020 base.

Other Census figures describe a growing, mostly owned housing stock.
