What are the 2026 tax rates and how is a Montgomery County bill calculated?

The Trustee's FAQ gives the 2026 county rate as $2.10 per $100 of assessed value, and Clarksville's FAQ lists the city rate as $1.01. A property inside the city therefore carries a combined $3.11 per $100.

Assessed value is a share of appraised value that depends on use: residential and farm are 25%, commercial and industrial 40%, personal property 30%, and public utilities 55%. The Trustee's method is to multiply the appraisal by the class percentage, divide by 100, then multiply by the rate.

What are the payment dates and late charges on a Montgomery County bill?

Bills are mailed during the final week of October. The window opens the first Monday in October and closes on the last day of February with no interest. After that, each month from March 1 adds 1.5 percent to the base tax, an annual 18 percent.

State law does not make the Trustee mail notices, and the county says a bill that never arrived is no defense for lateness. Partial payments toward the current year start July 10, as long as the balance is paid by the February cutoff. A payment mailed through the Postal Service counts on its postmark date, but office meter stamps do not count.

Online e-checks carry a 1.75 percent plus $1 charge, and Visa or MasterCard payments carry 2.65 percent plus $1. Cash works only at the counter. Several local banks accept current-year payments through February 28 when you show the original bill or a copy from the Trustee's website.

Clarksville adds its own steps for city tax. After a full year of delinquency the city passes the account to its delinquent tax attorney, and later payments go to the Clerk and Master at the chancery court.

What is the path for contesting a Montgomery County valuation?

Phone the Assessor at 931-648-5709 before anything else. A wrong room count or land class is often settled in one call. Unresolved disputes go to the county equalization board, which starts its June session on the first business day of the month and continues until its docket is finished.

To get a time slot, call the Assessor between May 15 and May 31. Five property owners from around the county make up the board, and state law reserves two seats for Clarksville residents. You can appear yourself or send a relative, lawyer or authorized agent. Bring appraisals, repair bills and comparable assessments. Leave out talk of what you can afford, since the board weighs value only.

The decision letter normally arrives before July. If you still disagree, the State Board of Equalization takes the next appeal, which must reach it by August 1 or 45 days after the county mailing, whichever falls later. The Assessor lists 2029 as the year of the next countywide reappraisal.

What tax relief and special bills affect a Montgomery County sale?

State relief repays a portion of the tax for low-income elderly and disabled owners and for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. In Clarksville, the Trustee's office is where you sign up for the Tax Freeze program, and relief applications are available at both the county Trustee and the city Finance and Revenue Department. Approved owners get a voucher with each bill and must send it in every year to both offices.

Greenbelt land brings another charge. If a sale ends the farm, forest or open-space classification, rollback taxes for the previous three years (five for open space) come due, and unless the contract says otherwise the seller owes them. A buyer who promises to keep the classification has 90 days after the sale to file the form with the Assessor, or the rollback becomes the buyer's problem. Unpaid rollback tax is a first lien on the land either way.

How does Montgomery County tax get settled at a closing?

New owners are told by the Trustee to check the closing statement or ask the title company who owes the year's tax. The lien-like effect is the key point: unpaid tax keeps accruing against the house whatever the purchase contract says. Clarksville's FAQ goes further and warns that a delinquent property can still end up at a tax auction.

Request a balance from the Trustee for county tax and from city Finance and Revenue for city tax. Find out whether your lender already paid from escrow, because the city refunds a double payment to whoever paid last. Then have the title company pay any remaining balance out of the seller's proceeds.

What are the 2026 property tax rates in Montgomery County?

What is the deadline to pay Montgomery County tax without interest?

The last day of February. The window opens on the first Monday of October. From March 1, 1.5 percent a month is added to the base tax.

Where do I start if my Montgomery County valuation looks too high?

Call the Assessor at 931-648-5709. If that fails, book a June hearing with the County Board of Equalization between May 15 and June 1, and use the State Board of Equalization after that.

Does a Clarksville house owe both city and county tax?

Yes. The Trustee collects only the county share, and the city bills its own. Homes outside the city limits owe the county portion alone.

Who owes the tax when a Montgomery County house sells?

The sale contract and the closing statement settle that between buyer and seller. The tax follows the calendar year and the property itself, so the title company should confirm the split and clear any balance at closing.

Who handles property tax in Roane County?

Three courthouse offices touch a Roane County tax bill, and all sit at 200 E. Race Street in Kingston. The Assessor of Property values the land, the Trustee collects the money, and the Clerk and Master takes over if the bill goes unpaid long enough to reach court.

  • Assessor of Property, Suite 5, 865-376-4362: values, ownership updates, greenbelt and tax freeze paperwork
  • Trustee, Suite 4, 865-376-4938 (mail to P.O. Box 296, Kingston, TN 37763): bills, payments, tax relief applications
  • Clerk and Master, Suite 12, 865-376-2487: delinquent taxes after a lawsuit is filed

The Trustee's page states that the Trustee does not set the rate or the appraisal. That is a common point of confusion. If you disagree with a value, you go to the Assessor and the county Board of Equalization. If you disagree with a rate, note that the assessor's page puts rate setting with the County Commission.

What are the 2026 property tax rates in Roane County?

A house inside a city pays the county rate of $1.4523 plus that city's rate, per $100 of assessed value. A house outside every city pays the rural county rate of $1.4987. Tennessee assesses residential property at 25 percent of appraised value.

Treat the results as an illustration. Your parcel's own appraisal and any exemptions drive the real bill.

When are Roane County property taxes due?

Taxes are due to the Trustee on October 1, according to the Assessor's calendar. The Trustee says notices normally go out in late September and the tax is payable through the end of February. The bill becomes delinquent on March 1.

Many owners wait until winter, and that is allowed. If the house is for sale, though, an unpaid bill from the current year shows up in the title search and gets paid at closing. A seller who pays in the fall removes one item from the settlement statement.

Where can you pay? The Trustee lists three routes. Online payment carries a convenience fee that the county does not keep. United Community Bank in Kingston and SimplyBank in Rockwood and Harriman take payments with no fee. The office also accepts partial payments when you pay in person.

How do assessments and appeals work in Roane County?

The Assessor values property as of January 1 and works on a four-year reappraisal cycle. Roane County's most recent reappraisal was the 2025 cycle. Values stay put between cycles unless the property changes physically, so a sale alone does not reset the number.

  • January 1: assessment date for ownership, assessments and tax maps
  • March 15: deadline to apply for greenbelt on land of 15 acres or more used for agriculture or forestry
  • May: assessment change notices go to owners whose appraisal changed
  • June 1: the County Board of Equalization begins hearing appeals
  • October 1: taxes are due to the Trustee

If your notice looks too high, call the Assessor at 865-376-4362 first and ask what comparable sales support the number. Take that to the Board of Equalization if the talk does not resolve it. Ask the office for the current filing deadline, because the board's schedule changes by year.

What tax relief and greenbelt options exist in Roane County?

Roane County offers three tools, each run through a different counter.

  • State tax relief for homeowners 65 or older, homeowners who are 100 percent disabled, certain service-connected disabled veterans and spouses of veterans killed in action. The Trustee handles the paperwork, the state decides eligibility, and the income limit changes each year.
  • The property tax freeze, adopted by the County Commission in 2007 under a state program. It is open to homeowners 65 or older under a state income limit, with no more than 5 acres, and the Trustee takes the annual application.
  • Greenbelt, filed with the Assessor by March 15, for farm or forest tracts of 15 acres or more.

Greenbelt carries a price on exit. When land stops qualifying, a roll-back charge equal to the taxes saved over the last three years comes due. A buyer or seller of a farm parcel should ask the Assessor whether greenbelt status is attached before a contract is signed.

What happens to delinquent Roane County taxes?

The Trustee's page says delinquent bills stay in its office for 18 months before they pass to the Clerk and Master. The delinquent tax page says a Chancery Court suit follows in March of the next year, with filing fees added and monthly interest still running. Ask both offices which one holds your year. Once the suit is filed, you pay the Clerk and Master and not the Trustee, and partial payments for a tax year are refused.

You can stop a sale by paying everything owed before the sale begins. The Clerk and Master asks for the map, group and parcel number and takes a business or cashier's check, a call to 865-376-2487, or an in-person payment. Call for a total, because interest adds on every month.

The county holds a back tax sale once a year at the courthouse. The next one is set for March 6, 2027. Property sells as is, bidders must be 18 or older and registered before the sale, and the court must confirm each sale. The usual redemption period is one year from the confirming order. For properties sold at the March 2027 sale where taxes are more than three years delinquent, a law effective July 1, 2026 cuts that to 90 days.

How do you sell a Roane County house with tax due?

Get a payoff, and pay it from the sale. The Trustee gives the figure while the bill is in its office, and the Clerk and Master gives it after a lawsuit.

  • Ask which office holds each year, since the answer decides where the check goes.
  • Give the closing agent the map, group and parcel number from your tax bill.
  • If you owe more than one year, request a total as of your closing date.
  • A city lot in Harriman, Kingston, Rockwood, Oak Ridge or Oliver Springs can carry a city charge as well, and the Clerk and Master collects delinquent city taxes too.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as is can close on a short timeline when the payoff is clean. That helps when a tax sale date is approaching.

What does Roane County look like for a seller?

Roane County covers 395 square miles, with 361 of land. Kingston is the county seat and Oak Ridge is the largest city. Harriman, Rockwood and Oliver Springs are the other incorporated places, and Midtown is a census-designated place. The Tennessee, Clinch and Emory rivers run through the county, mostly as Watts Bar Lake, and Walden Ridge rises on the Cumberland Plateau side.

The county was formed in 1801 and named for Archibald Roane, the second governor of Tennessee. Kingston is rooted in Fort Southwest Point, a frontier fort of the early 1790s. Rockwood became an iron and coal center, and Harriman was planned as a temperance town. Oak Ridge began in World War II as a Manhattan Project city, and the K-25 plant and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are in the county.

The Census Bureau counts 57,395 people on July 1, 2025, up 7.2 percent from the 2020 base. It lists 26,696 housing units and a 78.1 percent owner-occupancy rate. Median household income is $71,885, median rent is $785, and 24.6 percent of residents are 65 or older. That is the oldest population of the four Tennessee counties in the Census comparison table. The county issued 380 building permits in 2025.

When are Roane County property taxes due?

October 1 is the due date on the Assessor's calendar, and the tax is payable through the end of February. Unpaid bills become delinquent on March 1.

What is the 2026 Roane County property tax rate?

The county rate is $1.4523 per $100 of assessed value for city residents and $1.4987 outside the cities. City rates add to the county rate: Rockwood $0.6265, Harriman $0.7024, Kingston $0.8234, Oliver Springs $0.92 and Oak Ridge $1.3784.

Where can I pay Roane County property tax in person?

At the Trustee's office in the Courthouse, 200 E. Race Street, Suite 4, Kingston, or at United Community Bank in Kingston or SimplyBank in Rockwood and Harriman, where no fee is charged. Online payments carry a convenience fee.

When is the next Roane County tax sale?

The Clerk and Master lists the next Back Tax Sale for March 6, 2027. You can pay delinquent taxes up to the day of the sale, before it begins, to take a parcel off the list.

Can I freeze my Roane County property tax?

Possibly. Homeowners 65 or older with income under the state limit and no more than 5 acres can apply to the Trustee for the tax freeze each year. Call 865-376-4938 for the form and the current limit.

Tipton County by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Tipton County?

Three separate offices touch a Tipton County tax bill. The Assessor, Will Carter, values every parcel. The county commission and each city council set rates. The Trustee mails the bills and takes the money. The Assessor's own page lists three things the office does not do: it does not set the rate, send bills or collect taxes.

The Trustee works from 1 Pleasant Avenue, Room 203, in Covington (mailing address PO Box 487, Covington, TN 38019), phone 901-476-0211, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00. During tax season a second counter opens at Munford City Hall, 1397 Munford Avenue, every Wednesday from the first Wednesday in October through February 24, 2027, with Veterans Day and December 23 skipped. Questions about value or a mailing address go to the Assessor at 901-476-0213, the number the City of Covington gives on its tax page.

City tax is separate. The Trustee's page says city taxes are not collected at the county counter, and it lists the municipal offices:

How does Tipton County's setting shape home values?

Tipton County sits on the western edge of Tennessee, with the Mississippi River as its western boundary and Covington as the county seat. It covers 473 square miles, was formed on October 29, 1823 from part of Shelby County, and belongs to the Memphis metropolitan area. U.S. Highway 51 runs north to south through Covington. The county also lies on the southeastern edge of the New Madrid Seismic Zone, which Wikipedia notes as an area of high earthquake risk.

Towns inside the county are Atoka, Brighton, Burlison, Garland, Gilt Edge and Mason, plus the cities of Covington and Munford. Covington's South Main Historic District keeps about 50 homes from the late 1800s and early 1900s, and the district is federally registered.

  • Population of 62,287 as of July 2025, a 2.2% rise since April 2020

  • Household income around $74,127, with workers averaging 32.9 minutes to get to a job
  • Only 139 building permits in 2025

How is a Tipton County tax bill figured?

The Assessor sets an appraised value, the state assessment ratio turns that into assessed value, and the rate is applied per $100. The Assessor's page gives the ratios: residential 25 percent, farm 25 percent, commercial and industrial 40 percent, personal property 30 percent, public utility 55 percent.

Take a house appraised at $200,000. At 25 percent the assessed value is $50,000. At the 2026 rate of $1.3417 per $100, the county bill comes to roughly $671. At the 2025 rate of $1.5217 the same house would have owed about $761. The rate has fallen steadily in the history the Trustee posts:

How long can I wait to pay Tipton County tax before interest begins?

Billing opens on the first Monday in October, and the interest-free period runs through the last day of February. On March 1 the account is delinquent. The Trustee then adds 1.5 percent on the first of each month and rounds to the nearest dollar. Its schedule reads 1.5 percent in March, 3.0 in April and 4.5 in May, reaching 18.0 percent in February of the following year and 19.5 in March.

The notice leaves the office in the first week of October, addressed to the January 1 owner. A deed recorded ahead of the September deadline earns the new owner a copy too. Because today is November 15, 2026, a 2026 bill is open and no interest has started. The Trustee takes payment in these ways:

  • At the Covington counter, or at the Wednesday Munford counter during the season
  • Online through the Trustee's payment portal, where the vendor adds 2.5 percent on a card or $1.25 on an online check
  • By phone at 1-855-548-3603, with a $0.30 processing fee on top of the vendor charges
  • By bank draft, either in one annual payment, in four payments from November to February, or monthly, arranged at 901-476-0211

Partial payments are welcome, but interest is added to whatever remains after February 28. A refund is only issued on a parcel that another agency, such as a lender, has paid already. No other reason qualifies.

What is the route for disputing a Tipton County value?

A Tipton County owner who thinks the roll overstates a house has two steps. First comes the local County Board of Equalization. The Assessor posts the roll for public viewing in May and mails notices on parcels whose value moved, and the board's ruling closes out the roll for that year. Second comes Nashville, where the state's equalization board takes a filing up to August 1, or 45 days after the local notice went out, whichever is later. August 1 has already gone by for 2026, so read the date printed on your notice.

Facts and numbers carry a hearing. The state's guidance names three kinds of proof:

  • Recent sales of look-alike homes nearby, with adjustments for size, age and condition
  • A written appraisal from a professional who is ready to testify
  • Your own figure for the value, backed by reasons

Pay the part of the tax you do not dispute before March 1, along with any older delinquent tax. The State Board's phone line is 615-401-7883.

What property tax relief is available in Tipton County?

The state reimburses part or all of the tax for low-income elderly and disabled homeowners, disabled veterans, and widows or widowers of disabled veterans. The state's page dates the program to 1973. The Trustee's 2026 income cap is $38,470 from every source, for the applicant, spouse and any other owner, measured on 2025 income. Because it is a reimbursement and not an exemption, the bill is paid first.

Paperwork differs by group. Elderly applicants bring 2025 income proof and a Medicare or Social Security card. Disabled applicants bring proof of age plus a benefits letter when the payer is not Social Security. Veterans sign an F-16 and show ID. Mobile home owners add a title, bill of sale or affidavit of affixation. The office begins the 2026 process in October, so call 901-476-0211 to book.

What becomes of the 2026 bill if a Tipton County house sells?

The January 1 owner is on the roll, so a house sold in the fall still carries a bill in the seller's name. At closing the title company normally splits the year, and the buyer takes over from there. A seller with unpaid tax should ask the Trustee for the exact payoff, including any interest, before setting a closing date.

Pay at the Trustee's office at 1 Pleasant Avenue, Room 203, in Covington, or on Wednesdays at Munford City Hall during tax season. Online, phone and bank draft payments are also offered by the Trustee.

Only on a parcel that another agency has already paid, such as a lender. The Trustee says refunds are not issued for any other reason.

The Assessor's line is 901-476-0213. That office can talk through a value and explain how to get on the county board's schedule.

What should a seller know about Greene County, Tennessee?

Greene County fills a wide stretch of Tennessee's eastern border, with Greeneville serving as the seat and the biggest town. Its 624 square miles are almost entirely land. Settlers organized it in 1783 from Washington County, North Carolina, and gave it the name of Revolutionary War general Nathanael Greene. Davy Crockett was born here in 1786, and Tusculum is home to what Wikipedia calls the oldest college in Tennessee.

Long ridges and narrow valleys make up most of the terrain. Bays Mountain marks much of the line with Hawkins County on the north, and the far southeast corner rises into the Bald Mountains along the North Carolina border. The Nolichucky River runs through the southern half and backs up behind Nolichucky Dam into Davy Crockett Lake. Interstate 81, US 11E and US 321 are the main highways.

Tusculum is the county's one city, and Baileyton, Greeneville and Mosheim are towns. Greeneville City Schools covers addresses inside the Greeneville limits, while Greene County Schools serves everything outside them. Buyers ask about that line early, so know which district your street falls in.

Census QuickFacts gives this snapshot of the county:

  • 33,581 housing units, and 77.1 percent of households own their home
  • Typical owner-occupied value of $207,500 across 2020 to 2024, with monthly owner costs of $1,150 for those with a mortgage and $361 for those without
  • Household income of $56,194 and 16.3 percent of residents under the poverty line

Which Greene County offices handle property tax?

Three local bodies split the work. An elected assessor decides what each parcel is worth, the county commission chooses the rate, and the elected trustee mails the bill and banks the payment. The trustee's page says plainly that the trustee has no say in how large a bill is.

Trustee Nathan Holt works out of the Greene County Government Administration Center, 401 Takoma Avenue, Suite 104, Greeneville, TN 37743, on 423-798-1705. Hours run Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. The county technical assistance service lists Assessor of Property Chuck Jeffers at 401 Takoma Avenue, Suite 106, on 423-798-1738.

The Town of Greeneville taxes property too. Its Recorder's Office accepts those payments, so a home inside town limits generates a county bill and a town bill. For addresses in Mosheim, Baileyton or Tusculum, ask who collects the municipal share. The Comptroller says a city's collecting official may be its treasurer, its recorder or the county trustee.

How is a Greene County property tax bill figured?

The Trustee gives the formula as assessed value times the rate, divided by $100. Tennessee sets the assessed value at 25 percent of appraised value for homes and farms and 40 percent for commercial and industrial property.

The Trustee's own example takes a $25,000 assessed value and a $1.8731 rate, producing $468.28 that rounds to $468. It is labeled as a sample only. Put a house at the county's typical $207,500 and the assessed figure lands at $51,875. Multiply by the current rate and divide by 100 to get the county share. Ask the Trustee for the rate in force, since the commission and the town set theirs on their own schedules.

The Trustee also explains where the revenue goes. Property tax is the biggest local source for the general fund, with the wheel tax second. The school fund leans mostly on state education dollars, followed by property tax and local sales tax.

When is Greene County property tax due and how can I pay it?

Collection for the 2026 county bills began on Monday, October 5, 2026 and continues interest-free into late winter. Bills turn delinquent on March 1. As of November 15, 2026, the bill is open and not yet late.

The county mails a notice, though state law does not make it do so. A missing notice is no defense against interest. Call 423-798-1705 if yours never came, and call the Assessor on 423-798-1738 to correct your address on file.

The Trustee accepts payment these ways:

  • By mail, with the stub enclosed and the receipt number noted on the check, and a postmark is accepted
  • By phone at 1-833-591-7184 or online at tnproptax.com
  • Through the deposit slot just inside the Administration Center's main entrance

What is the path for contesting a Greene County property value?

Your first stop is the county's equalization board, which starts hearing cases on June 1 each year. Skip it and the value generally stands. The Assessor's office is where you ask to be scheduled.

An owner who loses there can carry the case to the State Board of Equalization. The filing window closes August 1 of that tax year, or 45 days after the county board mailed its decision if that comes later. A state judge holds a hearing and rules in writing within 90 days. You carry the burden of showing the right number, and you can reach the state board at 615-401-7883.

  • An appraiser's report, with the appraiser ready to appear
  • A concrete dollar value you propose, since simply calling the house overvalued rarely works

Meanwhile, pay the undisputed share of the bill by the delinquency date and settle any prior-year balances, or the case may be stalled or thrown out.

Which tax breaks can Greene County homeowners use?

Tennessee runs a refund-style relief program for low-income seniors, disabled owners, disabled veterans and certain surviving spouses. In 2026 an elderly or disabled applicant's 2025 income cannot exceed $38,470, and the refund is worked out on no more than $33,600 of market value. For veterans the cap on value is $175,000. Applicants must own and occupy the home, and seniors must turn 65 by December 31, 2026.

Because it reimburses taxes already paid, you still settle the bill first. Greene County's Trustee takes applications from the first Monday of October through March and wants a phone call beforehand to list the documents. The state brochure ties the final date to 35 days past delinquency, so confirm the exact day with the office.

A separate local-option freeze exists for owners 65 and up. The Comptroller's list of 28 adopting counties does not include Greene, so ask the Trustee if that changed.

What happens to the bill when a Greene County house sells?

According to the Trustee, the buyer and seller normally divide the year's tax at the closing table, and the Trustee's staff takes no part in that split. The title company or closing agent does the math and shows it on the settlement statement.

If you owe back tax, get a payoff figure from the Trustee early because interest keeps building. Sellers dealing with an inherited home, a vacant property or a long repair list can ask the title company to pay the balance out of proceeds. Recording the deed and the $0.37 per $100 state transfer tax happen at the register of deeds when the deed is recorded.

More questions about Greene County, TN Property Tax Guide

What is the Greene County property tax rate?

Call the Trustee at 423-798-1705 for the current figure, since the county commission and the Town of Greeneville each set a rate. The formula is assessed value times the rate divided by 100, with homes assessed at 25 percent of appraised value.

When do Greene County property taxes go delinquent?

March 1. Payments for 2026 were accepted starting October 5, 2026 and carry no interest through the end of February. After that, interest is charged until the balance is cleared.

Who should I contact about my Greene County property value?

The Assessor of Property at 423-798-1738, at 401 Takoma Avenue, Suite 106 in Greeneville. That office answers value questions, updates mailing addresses and starts the process toward the county equalization board.

Can seniors in Greene County get a tax break?

Yes, through the state relief program if 2025 income was $38,470 or less and the applicant owns and lives in the home. The Trustee takes applications. The local freeze exists only where a county adopted it, and Greene is not on the state's list.

Who pays the property tax at a Greene County closing?

Both sides, by proration. The Trustee says taxes are typically prorated at closing and that its own office does not split them. Your title company or closing agent does it.

If your value changed, call the assessor and ask what the new appraisal is based on, and ask the Trustee what rate applies to your 2026 bill.

Tennessee applies the same assessment ratios in every county: 25 percent of appraised value for residential and farm property and 40 percent for commercial and industrial. Keep any written value evidence, such as a recent appraisal or a sale of a comparable house nearby, and bring it to the assessor's office when you ask for an appointment.

Two other state dates matter for owners with land or rentals. The deadline to apply for greenbelt classification is March 15, and the deadline to apply for exemptions is May 20. Owners of business property, including equipment in a rental business, receive personal property schedules by February 1 and should return them by March 1.

What relief, delinquent tax and closing rules apply in Carter County?

Tennessee's tax relief program reimburses low-income elderly and disabled homeowners and disabled veteran homeowners or their surviving spouses for part or all of the local taxes paid. Elizabethton adds that prior-year city taxes must be paid or eligibility is lost.

The county Trustee's page says taxes over 13 months past due must be settled through the Clerk and Master at 423-542-1812, and tax sales are run by the Carter County Clerk and Master. For a payoff on a delinquent parcel, call the Trustee at 423-542-1811.

On a sale, the city's guidance is direct. A buyer or seller who closes after January 1 still sees the bill go to the owner of record as of that date, and the closing statement should deduct the former owner's pro-rata share. Taxes are a lien on the real property, and the purchaser is responsible for checking that earlier years were paid.

Carter County sits in the Blue Ridge Mountains, with Roan Mountain, at 6,285 feet, on the border with North Carolina. The Census Bureau counts about 57,361 residents, 28,715 housing units, a 75.2 percent owner-occupancy rate and a median household income of $50,135, so tax relief matters in a county where 24.1 percent of residents are 65 or older.

Pay the County Trustee at 801 East Elk Avenue, Elizabethton, or search and pay on citisenportal.com. City of Elizabethton taxes are paid separately at City Hall, 136 S. Sycamore Street.

Yes. The Tennessee Comptroller says relief is a state reimbursement, not an exemption. You receive the bill, pay it, and the state reimburses you for all or part of the taxes paid.

Which Dickson County offices set and collect property tax?

The assessor finds, lists and values every taxable parcel. The trustee sends the bills and takes the money. The twelve commissioners pick the rate when they adopt the budget.

What dates matter on a Dickson County tax bill?

The year runs from an assessment on January 1 to a payment window that opens in October and closes at the end of February. Most owners will see only the last two dates on this list, but the earlier ones explain when values can change.

What does a late Dickson County tax balance cost?

A balance still open on March 1 grows by one and a half percent every month, which the trustee describes as 18 percent over a year. The trustee holds it for twelve months and then passes the file to the Chancery Court and a delinquent tax attorney, which adds suit costs and fees on top of the interest.

At the end of that suit the county may sell the parcel at a tax sale. A seller who is behind should ask the title company to pay the arrears out of the sale proceeds before the file reaches court.

Bankruptcy is handled differently. Once a bankruptcy notice arrives, a deputy in the trustee's office files a claim, and federal law bars collection of real or personal property tax until the case is dismissed or discharged. Payment usually follows an installment plan approved by the bankruptcy court.

Who owes the tax when a Dickson County house changes hands?

The buyer inherits responsibility for anything left unpaid at closing, the trustee's FAQ says. How the current year's bill is divided is a matter for the purchase contract and the settlement statement.

After closing, the deed goes to the Register of Deeds, Shelly Yates, at 4 Court Square (P.O. Box 130, phone (615) 789-5123), who accepts electronic filings through Simplifile, CSC and ePN. Typos in an owner's name or mailing address on the bill are fixed through the assessor.

The General Assembly created Dickson County in October 1803, the twenty-fifth of Tennessee's 95 counties, out of land that belonged to Montgomery and Robertson counties. A tornado in 1833 flattened the courthouse square in Charlotte and, by Wikipedia's account, destroyed about 80 percent of the county's records. The replacement courthouse, finished in 1835, is the oldest in continuous use in the state.

The county covers 491 square miles, with the Cumberland River on its northeast side and the Harpeth River on the east. Iron furnaces drove early industry, railroads produced the towns of Dickson, Tennessee City, White Bluff and Burns, and U.S. Highway 70, known as the Broadway of America, crosses it. Montgomery Bell State Park, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the early 1940s, is a short drive east of Dickson. The county school district runs sixteen schools, and Tennessee College of Applied Technology and Nashville State Community College both have campuses in Dickson.

Anyone selling a house with tax owing, an inherited house or one needing work can get the balance and the valuation from the trustee and assessor in two calls.

When can I start paying Dickson County property tax?

From the first Monday of October. Payment without interest is accepted through the last day of February, and March 1 starts the delinquent period.

At the trustee's counter in the Charlotte courthouse square or the branch at 303 Henslee Drive in Dickson, from eight to four on weekdays. Mail goes to P.O. Box 246, Charlotte, TN 37036, and local banks take full current-year payments.

You can, because the purchaser is responsible for tax unpaid at closing. Check the settlement statement to see how the year's tax was prorated between you and the seller.

Homeowners 65 or older and disabled homeowners with 2025 income at or below $38,470, plus disabled veterans and certain surviving spouses with no income limit. The application goes to the Dickson County Trustee.

What does the Madison County landscape look like to a seller?

Madison County lies in West Tennessee, and Jackson is its seat and its biggest city. It was founded in 1821 and named for James Madison. It covers 559 square miles, nearly all land, and borders Gibson, Carroll, Henderson, Chester, Hardeman, Haywood and Crockett counties. Interstate 40 crosses it along with US 45, US 70 and US 412.

Several landmarks shape how people describe the area. Pinson Mounds, one of the largest Woodland period mound complexes in the country, lies in the county, and Lake Graham, a 500-acre reservoir, sits five miles east of Jackson. Beyond Jackson, the county includes Medon, Three Way, Beech Bluff, Pinson and parts of Humboldt and Mercer. The Jackson-Madison County School System serves public school families, Lane College and Union University are in the county, and West Tennessee Healthcare runs the public hospital system. Jackson Regional Airport took that name in 2025.

When does the next Madison County reappraisal happen?

Madison County works on a five-year cycle, and between cycles the office inspects about one-third of the parcels each year for changes to land or buildings.

The office posts a market indicator on that page. It reports a median residential sale price of $251,450 as of January 2026, against $212,500 at the 2022 reappraisal, which it describes as roughly an 18.33% rise. That gap is the main reason an owner should expect a higher appraised value in 2027. The board is five property owners from the county and the City of Jackson. One FAQ elsewhere on the county site says the board sits for the first week to ten days of June, so confirm the dates with the Assessor. The county asks residential owners to bring comparable sales from the year or two before the tax year, a recent paid appraisal and photos of the exterior and interior. Owners of income property are asked for three years of leases, rent rolls, income and expenses, appraisals, sales contracts, closing statements and construction costs. Refusing to supply those documents can cost the right to introduce them before the State Board. The appeal page adds that the State Board filing carries a fee, with $10 to $17 of it nonrefundable, and that you must pay at least the undisputed part of the tax before it turns delinquent. The State Board's number is 615-401-7883.

What tax relief does the Madison County Trustee offer?

The Trustee takes applications for the state's relief program for elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans. Call the Trustee's office at (731) 423-6027 for the current requirements.

Applicants should bring a driver's license, a Medicare card, a Social Security card and proof of income for the applicant, spouse and every owner of the property. A mobile home owner also needs a copy of the title or bill of sale. Because the dollar limits change from year to year, ask the Trustee for the current income cap and filing deadline before assuming you qualify.

Ask the Trustee, and the Jackson Revenue Office if the house is in the city, for a written balance before you list. Mcminn County by the numbers

Where do McMinn County owners go with property tax questions?

Tax bills come from the Trustee, and value questions go to the Assessor of Property. The Trustee works from the courthouse in Athens, and the County Commission sets the rate.

  • Trustee: McMinn County Courthouse, 6 East Madison Avenue, Athens, TN 37303. Phone (423) 745-1291, fax (423) 744-1603.
  • Hours: Weekdays, 8:00 to 4:00, plus Saturday mornings in February, 8:30 to noon.
  • Assessor of Property: appraises and classifies each parcel, verifies sales and handles reappraisal questions.

The Trustee's page lists the three jobs of the office: collecting county property tax, keeping the county's accounts, and investing idle funds. It also runs the state tax relief program for elderly and disabled owners and disabled veterans. Tax notices are mailed in October to whoever owned the property on January 1, and the owner is responsible for keeping the mailing address current with the Assessor.

What is McMinn County like for a homeowner or seller?

McMinn County sits in East Tennessee, and Athens is both its seat and its biggest city. It was created in 1819 and named for Governor Joseph McMinn. It covers 432 square miles of Ridge and Valley country, where long parallel ridges run northeast to southwest. The Hiwassee River marks the line with Bradley County, and Starr Mountain rises in the southeast along the edge of the Cherokee National Forest.

Besides Athens, the county holds the cities of Etowah, Niota and Sweetwater, the towns of Calhoun and Englewood, and Riceville. Railroads shaped the early map: the East Tennessee and Georgia line ran through in the 1850s, Etowah grew around an L&N depot, and Englewood became a textile town. In 1946, returning World War II veterans confronted county officials over a disputed election in the Battle of Athens.

School lines matter here. McMinn County Schools runs most of the public schools, including McMinn County High and McMinn Central High. Athens City Schools and the Etowah School District cover grades K to 8 in their own areas, with the county's high schools taking those students after eighth grade. Tennessee Wesleyan University is in Athens.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for McMinn County:

  • Population on July 1, 2025: 57,404, up 7.8% from April 2020
  • Housing units: 24,424, with 75.8% owner-occupied from 2020 to 2024
  • Typical owner-occupied house, by value: $211,800
  • Median gross rent: $803, and median household income $61,470
  • Building permits in 2025: 125

What is the McMinn County property tax rate for 2026 to 2027?

The combined county rate is $1.0823 per $100 of assessed value for the fiscal year that began July 1, 2026. The County Commission set it by Resolution 26-036 at its June 15, 2026 meeting, and the Trustee is authorized to round tax statements to the nearest whole dollar. Assessments follow state classes: 25 percent for farm and residential property, 30 percent for personal property, 40 percent for industrial and commercial property and 55 percent for public utilities.

The levy splits across six funds. Three of the lines carry school names: McMinn, Athens and Etowah.

As a worked example, a house appraised at $211,800, the county's median owner-occupied value, has an assessed value of $52,950. Multiply that by $1.0823 per $100 and the county tax comes to about $573. A city may add its own tax, so the figure covers county tax only.

When are McMinn County property taxes due?

Payment opens October 1 and stays open through the last day of February without penalty. Today is November 15, 2026, so the current year's tax is already payable. On March 1 the Trustee adds 1.5 percent per month in penalty and interest to unpaid tax.

Mail is accepted, and the postmark sets the payment date, with a receipt returned by mail. Delinquent tax is a lien that follows the parcel to any owner, so buyers are urged to run a title check for liens. The county also requires delinquent taxes to be paid before current ones, which means a prior-year balance absorbs a payment aimed at this year's bill.

The office also opens on Saturday mornings in February. For payment methods beyond mail and in-person, call (423) 745-1291.

How can a McMinn County owner dispute a value?

Start with the Assessor of Property, then file with McMinn County's local equalization board. State law sends a disputed value to the county board before anything else, and a case that skips it generally becomes final. The Comptroller's appeals guide explains that the county board is a panel of five or more people who hear complaints and can change disputed assessments.

  • County board: file by the date the Assessor gives you for this year's session.
  • State Board of Equalization: on August 1, or on the 45th day after the county board mailed its notice if that is later.
  • Hearing: before an administrative judge, with a written decision within 90 days after the hearing.
  • Chancery court: a petition within 60 days after the state board's order is final.

McMinn County's FAQ adds one point for business owners. A forced assessment, which happens when a business fails to file a personal property schedule, can be set aside only by an appeal to the local board before that year's deadline. The county's FAQ says the schedule is due before March 1.

What property tax relief exists for McMinn County owners?

The Trustee administers a state-funded program for elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans. When an applicant qualifies, the State of Tennessee pays a portion of the tax on the home. The Trustee's page says an application must be filed no later than 35 days after the February 28 payment deadline, which lands in early April. The FAQ also mentions programs for veterans with a 100 percent rating.

Because income limits and credit amounts are set by the state each year, call (423) 745-1291 for this year's figures before you apply.

What should a McMinn County seller know about tax at closing?

Old tax stays with the house, so a buyer's title search will find any unpaid year. The county says delinquent tax binds the property whoever owns it, and a seller with a late balance should expect the title company to require payoff at closing.

Ask the Trustee for the amount for each tax year, including interest, before you accept an offer. If the house is inherited, behind on payments or in need of repairs, the tax balance is one more number the title company will collect from the proceeds, and knowing it early keeps the closing date from slipping.

More questions about McMinn County, TN Property Tax Guide

What is the current McMinn County property tax rate?

The combined county rate is $1.0823 for every $100 of assessed value, covering the fiscal year that started July 1, 2026. The County Commission adopted it on June 15, 2026. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value.

When does McMinn County charge interest on late taxes?

On and after March 1. The Trustee adds 1.5 percent per month to delinquent tax, and payment is open from October 1 through the last day of February without penalty.

Can I mail my McMinn County property tax?

Yes. Mailed payments are accepted and the postmark date decides whether you paid on time. The Trustee returns a receipt by mail.

Which school systems affect a McMinn County tax bill?

Three funds on the levy support schools: McMinn, Athens and Etowah. Athens City Schools and the Etowah School District serve grades K to 8 in their areas, while McMinn County Schools covers most of the rest.

Do I need to pay old McMinn County taxes before this year's?

Yes. The Trustee's FAQ says delinquent taxes must be paid before current taxes can be paid. A delinquent balance also attaches to the parcel whoever owns it.
